newsitem.title: USA: Short-term stress would not mean Russia cut - S&P.
newsitem.headline: Short-term stress would not mean Russia cut - S&P.

text.p: Standard and Poor's said Thursday that a short period of policy stress in Russia would not affect the country's debt service ability or lead the agency to downgrade the country's credit rating.
Helena Hessel, director of sovereign ratings at S&P, said on a teleconference that the agency would be watching closely how long periods of stress would last.

"Short periods of policy stress would not affect Russia's ability to service its debt. Short periods of stress would not lead us to downgrade our rating or put it on Creditwatch," she said. "We would be watching to see how long the stress lasts."

She added that S&P would look closely at any potential stresses in the relationship between Russia and the International Monetary Fund, and if any strain in the relationship became prolonged, then the country's rating could come under pressure.
On Monday, S&P rated Russia's long-term foreign currency debt at BB-minus and noted the country's strong backing by international organizations, as well as its debt rescheduling.
"Our ratings are supported by our belief that there is and will be strong support from international organizations including the IMF," Hessel said.
Hessel noted that she expected the multilateral institutitons would have a high exposure in Russia over the next few years.
S&P also would need to resolve key legal questions about the Russian Federation's support for Russian Vneshekonombank dollar-denominated paper before deciding on credit ratings, Hessel said.

"We are in the process of looking at what will be the status of these bonds from the legal point of view," Hessel said. "We are actually looking at the legal language of the federation as far as the rescheduling is concerned."
Regarding Russia's rating assignment, S&P said the country's "manageable" external debt profile helped to boost the credit rating.
"The maturity structure of debt is very beneficial, and strong in the Russian Federation," Hessel said. "There is very little short term debt, which is usually vulnerable to investor perceptions."

The "unusual" levels of support from the international community for the country's transition had also been very important to the rating, Hessel said. "We believe that support from the IMF will be very strong."
Still, Russia faces several serious challenges, such as finding ways to increase tax collection, which would be politically difficult.
Also constraining the rating would be the weak legal system and the short track record of economic management, she said.
